utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-04-74-T.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to everybody, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused. Before we bring in the witness, we have a very brief oral decision, the decision on admission of evidence introduced through Witness CH. He appeared in the hearing of 28th November, 2001. The Prosecution tendered exhibits that we decided to admit, P 09749 under seal, admitted because they are of relevance and have certain probative value. P 09760 under seal, P 03134, P 03105, P 03110. The Chamber reminds you that P 03075 has already been admitted through Witness CE. The Chamber notes that the Defence did not tender any evidence, any exhibits. I would now like the usher to drop the blinds and bring in our witness. Meantime, the registrar will give us the IC number for the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] Through Witness CN will be given IC 169. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. While the witness is being brought in, perhaps if we could make a quick inquiry from the Stojic and Coric Defence teams with respect to whether or not they will be filing a response concerning the Prosecution appeal of the decision cutting the time for the Prosecution. I ask because the Prosecution may seek leave to reply in the course of that appeal, and we have yet to see responses from the Coric and Stojic teams. I'm just curious if they are going to be filing responses, and if so, perhaps we could get an indication as to when we might expect to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are consulting right now in order to make that decision, and we will make it within -- before the end of tomorrow, and we'll have course let know the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. You can sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you have 10 minutes left. Let me remind you we are in open session, so please be cautious.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will not refer to any names even though they can in no way identify the witness, but still, for the moment let us go into private session to avoid all problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the Territorial Defence in Stolac established in the spring of 1992 supposed to fight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against the Serbian aggressor that came to the plateau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, as a member the Territorial Defence, did you have a weapon, and, if you did, who did you get it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a weapon, and for the purposes of the Territorial Defence I was a driver on call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody else in the Territorial Defence was armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were few weapons, a negligible amount and negligible quality. Mainly hunting rifles. Because it was impossible to buy them and nobody could give them to us, because it was at the very beginning when the Serbian aggressor just arrived at the Dubrava plateau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had hunting rifles, privately owned weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they were probably licensed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A logical question arises: If the Territorial Defence, when the Serbian -- when the Yugoslav army arrived and later the Montenegrin army was equipped in such a way they were unable to put up any resistance or fight.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not until the HVO came to the Dubrava plateau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know from previous evidence that after reservists came from Montenegro, a large number of Muslims - and we know that Croats fled earlier - crossed over to the western part of Herzegovina and elsewhere by crossing the Neretva and in other ways. Did you join them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did cross over the Neretva and stayed there for a short while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me when and what was that short period of time that you spent elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that on the right bank of the Neretva in Medjugorje and in Ljubosko various units were being formed made up the Muslims and that they were training in that territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a few things about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign up into those units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had signed up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you part of those units? Did you train?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not train, but I was with them for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that those units received rifles and weapons, and do you know from whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the men with whom I was had received any weapons. They were turned back home a few days later. They had no weapons. You can check that. Maybe you have documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you say that you were there just a few days, are you speaking for yourself or do you know that the other groups didn't receive any weapons or training?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking for myself and the seven or eight people who were with me. I state with full responsibility that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know which units, which HVO units, took part in the liberation of Stolac in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please believe me when I say I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long the operation to liberate Stolac lasted in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which units of the BH army took part in the liberation of Stolac in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single unit of the BH army took part in that in June 1992. Not a single unit took part because the -- it didn't exist, the Bregava Brigade. There were just these members of the TO with the hunting rifles. Those people took part. And two or three men who had the money to buy rifles, they had them. As far as I know, those were the three men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn later on how many soldiers of the HVO were killed and how many wounded in the operation to liberate Stolac in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that three young guys, three or four -- I think it's three young guys were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about whether the -- Bajro Pizovic who was later commander of the Bregava Brigade took part in liberating Stolac from the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the HVO was composed of Croats and Muslims alike, that there were a large number of Muslims in its units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the HVO was a multi-ethnic army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Normally that was the case until you know what date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the Bregava Brigade of which you were a member, were there any Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Bregava Brigade. Well, there was not a single Croat in the Bregava Brigade to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did somebody from the HVO in any way whatsoever prevent the establishment of the Muslim Bregava Brigade of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I'm not well-versed in things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Bregava Brigade? Was it armed? Did people have weapons? Did they have mortars, boots, uniforms, RPGs, and the like, PATs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but to a lesser extent, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about 82-millimetre mortars? How many would you say? You said few of them, but how many do you say -- would you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any of these numbers or figures. I don't know how much of what there was. I didn't count anything. All I knew was to do my job, so I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, up at the brigade's positions, did you see an anti-aircraft gun, the PAT, at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a Zolja? Do you know what a Zolja is and an RPG is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bregava Brigade receive its weapons through the HVO from Croatia or from some other source?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I know nothing about things like that, where they got them from, how. That wasn't something that interested me, nor was it my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, since you were a driver --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- do you know where the ammunition came in from, from the brigade, because there was some shooting here and there. So where did the ammunition come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat once again that I don't know anything about things like that. I was in the town of Mostar driving around. I didn't go further than that general area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a question which probably you are best qualified to answer, Mr. Praljak. What is a Zolja? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] It's like this. It's an anti-armoured device, a very light device, just several kilogrammes. It's a hand-held rocket launcher. You can hold it on your shoulder. You have a tube, a barrel, and you can see them in the films. It's what the terrorists very often use to destroy cars, tanks, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I know that from my own shooting experience. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I know that the Swiss are duty-bound to protect their country and very often have weapons which they can keep at home, but I know that there were never any killings and deaths caused by the weapons they keep at home. They are such a highly disciplined nation, which unfortunately we -- well, at least that's what some sociological studies say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, whose trucks -- whose trucks were they that you drove? Did they belong to you privately or to some company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were my private vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about all the rest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the vehicles were privately owned, mostly. Not mostly but all of them, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me this, please: You said yesterday that you know what the -- the line that the -- the front line that the Bregava Brigade covered, how long was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CQ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really answer that. In kilometres I can't tell you. It's something I don't really know about. It went right up to the HVO, where the HVO held the line. I don't know how far that is or what distance it is, but I know that the lines were up at Rotimlja, and so on of the how long they were, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May we please go into private session for my next questions because I need to name names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the next witness require protective measures, Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe my colleague Mr. Poryvaev who is standing right outside would be in the best position to answer that question. If you could just give us a moment while we do a slight rotation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to greet Prosecutor Poryvaev. It's been a while since we've last saw you. It's a pleasure to have you back. Mr. Poryvaev, can you tell it us with the witness who is going to come in soon? Did he ask for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Ismet Poljarevic. He doesn't request any protective measures. He's ready to testify in open session. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that you planned to have one hour in direct examination. So the Defence would also have one hour normally. Let us ask the usher to bring the witness in. We are going to take a break at quarter past 5.00, because our normal schedule was slightly disrupted today. Let us use these few minutes. Registrar, let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Witness. I'm going to first check you can hear everything and whether you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please give me your first and last name, date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ismet Poljarevic, born on the 17th of May, '57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently I work in -- on a production line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified before, before a court concerning events that took place in your country between '92 and '94, or is it the first time you are appearing as a witness before a Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified already before a court in Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you testified before a court already in Germany. Was that a trial concerning the events in your country between '92 and '95, or does it concern something else entirely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it concerns those events, because it had to do with Ante Prlic, who was chief of the camp of Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This German court, did it bring in a verdict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you testified as a victim or as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I think I testified as a victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you please now read from the document given you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, since you already have some experience of courtrooms, you will realise that the procedure in Germany is very different from the one here in as much as the questions are not asked by the Judges but first by the Prosecution and then by Defence counsel, which doesn't mean that Judges, too, will not ask questions. Please try to be clear and precise in answering these questions, and very importantly, if you are talking about something you saw with your own eyes, emphasise that, as opposed to things that you heard or found out from others, from speaking to others. If you have any difficulty whatsoever, do not hesitate to let us know. The Prosecution will have one hour to question you. He will maybe show you documents related to his questions, after which Defence teams will have one hour to question you. All this will go very fast, and in the best of scenarios, you may not have to come back tomorrow, but perhaps you will. We do not know yet. We have 15 minutes left before the next break, and the Prosecution will begin their direct examination now, after which, in 15 minutes, we will have to take a break for technical reasons of about 20 minutes. The Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but short information about Witness Poljarevic, about hearings he took part in Germany. It was understood from his explanation yesterday it was a sort of preliminary hearing, not a full-fledged trial where he was brought under oath. So that was his court experience. Now, a short summary. Ismet Poljarevic lived in Sovici. He was a member of the local defence forces. On the 17th of April, 1993, when the Croatian Defence Council units from Jablanica attacked the village, in the morning the witness was in the village and saw some HVO soldiers and also saw some soldiers who were wearing HV uniform and insignia. The local Muslim unit commander Dzemal Ovnovic decided to surrender to the HVO and which most of his soldiers did. The men and women were separated from -- sorry, men and women were separated and imprisoned in the primary school in Sovici. The witness was interrogated by some HVO soldiers and was severely beaten. They also took away his and his brother vehicles and they were never given them back. Muslim men from the school building were transferred to the Ljubuski prison, then most of them were transferred to the Heliodrom prison. While being in the Ljubuski military prison, Ismet Poljarevic was involved in forced labour and also got information about Ljubuski inmates being beaten by the military police. On the 17th of May, 1993, Ismet Poljarevic with two other inmates was taken to Mostar on Ante Prlic order - Ante Prlic was commander of the Ljubuski military prison - and he was proposed to do some job for the HVO as a driver. Ismet Poljarevic refused to do this job, making reference to the fact that he knew the Mostar area pretty badly. Then he was taken to the mechanical faculty building which was used by the military police as a sort of headquarters where he was kept for about three days and was severely beaten. After that, the witness was returned to Ljubuski and at the end of May was transferred to Heliodrom. In Heliodrom the witness was kept until the 1st of March, 1994. That is my summary. And now some -- just questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Poljarevic, did you really give a statement to the OTP investigator on the 3rd of May, 1997?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you give the statement freely, of your own accord, and without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of the interview were you given to read the witness statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you tell the truth to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you sign your statement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown his witness statement. That's our Exhibit P 009726.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, it's in your binder. Please open it. That is an English version. Is it your signature in the English version?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday we had a meeting with you, and you make some corrections and amendments to your statement and also some, let's say, typing -- or errors were rectified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like to call attention of the Trial Chamber to the amendments made by -- by the witness. Yesterday, the Trial Chamber and the Defence were notified about these amendments and clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that in the school building, I mean Sovici school, you were interrogated by one of the HVO commanders named Ivan, and at that time the minutes were taken by a certain Azinovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that your wife and two children were transferred along with other civilians from Sovici to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that the name of detainee you eyewitness as being beaten in the Ljubuski military prison was Junuzovic Feriz?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness also wanted to amend his statement by the fact that after he had been released from Heliodrom in March 1994 he learned from his villagers that the four Muslim civilians from the Sovici school had been killed in the courtyard in the Sovici school. They were executed by the HVO soldier. Their names are Ismet Cilic, Hasan Rados, Salem Skampo, and Ekrem Tasic. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Poljarevic also added that Ibro Kukic had been wounded in the area between Stolac and Popovo Polje where he was taking part in the forced labour in the -- being taken from the Ljubuski military prison. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Muharem Cilic was wounded in Doljani in April 1993 and was also brought to the Ljubuski military prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In the military -- in the MUP station in Mostar, in the faculty, in the mechanical faculty building, he was beaten by the military police members with a flag pole. The people who were beating him were dressed in the HVO military police uniform. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Dzidic also known as Dzida, was the full name of a person who was in charge of the HVO military police at the MUP station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: There were also female detainees in Heliodrom who were kept in the central prison on the attic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: One of the guards of Heliodrom, Ante Buhovac, was the one who brought the detainees there. He belonged to the HVO military police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Detainees from Heliodrom were involved in forced labour on the confrontation line even in December 1993 and afterwards. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Detainees from Heliodrom Ismet Cilic, Rasim Cilic, Sefik Tasic, and Mustafa Tasic, who had also been arrested in Sovici, were killed while they were performing forced labour on the confrontation lines. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: HVO representatives before releasing detainees from Heliodrom were proposing that they should go to some third countries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Conditions of detention both in Ljubuski and Heliodrom were deplorable. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Ismet Poljarevic also made some slight corrections in the spelling of some names mentioned in the witness statement such as, for example, instead of Junozovic we should read Junuzovic in all cases. This full name mentioned in the statement for several people who are not the same persons, actually, but the spelling should be Junuzovic. And also one point that fell through the crack, on page 6 of the English version, in the first paragraph, a wrong word is used. It should be said that on one occasion the HVO soldiers threatened but not treated with cutting -- yes, to someone. It's just a mistake. Of course in the B/C/S version it's page 5, paragraph 5. Paragraph 5 it's also translated in that way, as though the ears had been cut, but in fact they were threatening with cutting ears. So, Your Honour, only one minute is left for the break. I think that we should take the break and then I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I may, Mr. President, with all due respect to my colleague, again this is another demonstration where valuable time was spent reading a list when, I do this for the benefit of the members of the Bench who were not here last week, but this is again another example where one question could be posed to the witness. This can be read to the witness outside. He can vouch for it, sign it, and this could be entered into evidence and we don't need to spend all this time. We will assume that these corrections then become part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mundis, in future it would be visible that after the proofing session, once you have corrected this type of document, you could just ask the witness a question and say, "You have made a certain number of corrections. We have made a list of those corrections in a document. Do you confirm?" For example, for this particular witness there were 14 corrections. And he can say "yes," and that would be the end of the matter and we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are dealing with just practical matters like that, I'm not sure, have the Prosecution now dropped the practice which I thought we'd established? An assurance was given to a question by Judge Trechsel the other day that if the summary was not exactly the same as the 65 ter summary it would be provided in advance, or was that? Because the trouble is otherwise we have to check. Was that summary simply a reading out of the 65 ter summary? It's just helpful to know these things in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The second point is that normally the 65 ter summary is communicated to the Defence. I saw it a while ago. It was done a while ago. But for the public, we need to have a reading of the 65 ter when it's -- when we're in open session. So, Mr. Mundis, on those two points, how do the Prosecution view them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll leave the second point regarding the 65 ter summary to my colleague, but with regard to the first point, certainly compiling a list is -- is one way of doing it, but of course due to time constraints we don't have the ability quite often to produce translations for the benefit of the witness with respect to the changes made to the document, so it's simply not possible in all situations to get the witness to sign a list of any changes or a revised version of the statement, which then requires us or necessitates the type of procedure that was used today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, what -- when Mr. -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Mr. Mundis, when you seat witness during the proofing session there's an interpreter who is there, and the interpreter could translate the document and then he can say -- the witness can say, "Yes, I've understood." Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Especially when the witness in court is shown a French version or English version which they've already initialled and they're asked, you know, can they verify it. I just think if it's read back to them orally and then they -- they initial it, we will accept that. I think it's a principled position that the Defence is taking. We honour, you know, that it will have been read, he signs it, we can move on. Happy ending. We can save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question, Your Honour, sorry. Yes. He didn't answer my question. A few days ago, Judge Trechsel asked specifically whether it was an assurance had been given -- if the summary was not going to be simply exactly the 65 ter summary the Defence, as we had requested, would be provided with in advance. And the answer was yes. It doesn't seem to be happening. I'm not quite sure who is in charge. When Mr. Mundis says, I leave it to my colleagues, we can't have inconsistent practises according to which Prosecution counsel happens to be dealing with the matter. We have to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But to clarify this, Mr. Mundis, but I'm sure you've understood. There are 65 ter summaries which are well known to one and all because they were seen out to the Defence. We're talking about the hypothesis where the 65 ter summary is different after the proofing session, that you change certain points after the proofing session, and everybody seemed to agree that should that happen, the Prosecution must then send to the Defence the amended version, the new version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My colleague informs me, Mr. President, that this -- what he read out came directly from the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's fine then. And if the practice is now consistently adopted in future that's into problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe what we've said is we would -- we would advise if it's different, and therefore if it's not different there will be no such notification given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And following on from Mr. Karnavas's suggestion to have the document in English initialed, just as the witnesses initial their written statement, could the accused proceed in that fashion. After the proofing session, read out the document through an interpreter and then the person can initial it and we can all save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, I will take all this under advisement and we'll see if we can adopt that. Again, it's not always possible because of the set-ups of the proofing rooms to have a computer. Not all of the rooms we use to proof have computers. Sometimes it's handwritten notes by the lawyer who then takes those back to his or her office and produces the letter that is then transmitted. But we will do our best to read those read those back to the witnesses, time permitting. Of course, that might result in situations where we're proofing in the morning and an afternoon hearing might have to be delayed so that we can we can do that with the witness. We will certainly endeavour to do that in order to expedite the proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we're going to have the recess soon, the registrar can furnish you with a portable computer and everything else that you need and then you could do this straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, we can certainly see about the availability of laptops. Of course people going on missions have first priority rather than simply using them in building but it's going to be -- I can assure you, Mr. President and Your Honours, as we move to a schedule with full utilisation of all the courtrooms, we're similarly stretched within the office space of the Office of the Prosecutor, in terms of rooms that we can use that are suitable to proof witnesses in. We will see about the availability of laptops and I can see about ensuring that this type of procedure is adopted. But again, it's primarily due to time constraints and resource constraints in terms of rooms that are available that may or may not make it possible in each and every instance to undertake this type of procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. It's 20 past 5.00. We're going to take a 20-minute break and reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, the summary read out was not the same as the 65 ter summary. I just say that, could we please as for simple, efficient, business-like implementation of the Prosecution assured the Trial Chamber they would do. It is simply not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Poryvaev, it seems that what you read out does not correspond to the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I don't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I just read not the whole thing from 65 ter but a shorter summary, which is more relevant to the case here. Nothing was added. Nothing was skipped. I mean important things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's not correct. Please. I just invite my learned friend to look at it this evening and see. It's different. He's added some words here. I'm not saying he didn't conscientiously attempt to base it on the summary. There is no allegation of sharp practice. It's just we want a business-like practice that the summary is supplied to us when it's different so we can see it, and we can avoid all this. This is about the fifth time that we've wasted this time. I don't want to be on my feet every few days asking for them please to do what they said they would do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, Mr. Scott and all the others representing the Prosecutor, it's very simple. When the summary is identical to the 65 ter summary, then there's no need to provide the contents to the Defence. However, when it is different, when it differs, as Mr. Poryvaev has just told us, because he changed a few words or abridged it, then it should be communicated to the Defence teams. So it's very simple. It seems very simple to me. Perhaps it's more complicated for the Prosecution, but it seems to me to be a very simple matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll do our best to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Poljarevic, if you were to give evidence again in full before this Tribunal, would what you say in your witness statement and the additional information given to us be your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender into evidence within statement of Ismet Poljarevic, Exhibit number P 09726.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have any documents to show him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown Exhibit P 02131.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: This is reported of the command of the police station dated April 28, 1993 about the engagement of Jablanica civilian police members in battalion units. Witness, I would like you to take a look at this document. Do you see it? Do you have your binder? Just open the corresponding number and -- or maybe it will be shown on the screen. Witness, have you read the document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: I haven't read it all yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While the gentleman is reading the document, Your Honour, if I could use this opportunity to once again make an observation that this is a document from -- from the HVO. Obviously the gentleman hasn't seen it. Again, I urge that the practice be adopted where the -- whereby a witness gives a narration and then if the Prosecution wishes to tender documents with the relevant sections to them, they can tie them in, link them, however you wish to call it. But I think this again demonstrates how we spend a lot of time in a procedure that is very much, you know, while it's adversarial, we're moving closer, closer to the continental procedure with these documents, and I think we're wasting valuable time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, he should have read the document yesterday with you. You should have shown the witness the document yesterday. Did you do so or not? Because if you're showing the witness a document today for the first time, the time it takes him to read is wasting our time. You should have done that work yesterday and then just asked him today this is a document that we saw yesterday, the two of us together. Do you know the document? And then the witness can say yes, and then you can go on and ask your questions on any of the paragraphs of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was shown a number of documents yesterday. Of course he should have some time to refresh his memory. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, do you see any of the people -- of the names of people who were familiar to you before in this document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: For example, who are the people who are mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: For example, Andrija Groznica, Andrija Pole, Ivan Groznica, Mato Mijic, Miro Stipanovic, and the other two seem familiar, but I can never remember their names, Vlado Rotim, and Milenko Drinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know what was their position in April 1993? What was their occupation, profession?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: They were at the position of attacking Sovici, and they were uniformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see them on the 17th of April in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Briefly, what happened and in which circumstances did you see them?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: They were rallying up the population, the Muslims, and searching the village and the houses, and as security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm going to the heart of the matter, the basic question that we want to know. The names you've indicated, did you know them before the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And on the 17th of April, 1993, you saw them in Sovici as they were gathering up the population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any personal contacts with them on that day?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th I had personal contact with Andrija Groznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What happened on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: He personally, with two other soldiers I didn't know, took me to search my house. They searched the house and confiscated my Peugeot 305 passenger vehicle, saloon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did they confiscate anything else?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in your language, in English and French it says "confiscated." Was it confiscated? Was it stolen? Was it requisitioned? Do you have a word that could characterise more precisely the situation involving your car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the best way that I can describe this is that they took away my car, confiscated it, and that I never saw it again. Under pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The word "confiscated," when one confiscates something you might confiscate a toy from a child but you return the toy later on, whereas your car was never returned to you, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, never. I never saw my car again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was taken away once and for all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was seized once and for all. Confiscated meaning seized, never to be returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, did you get any paper related to this car, a receipt, an attestation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't receive any paper or any oral explanation either. No receipt or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Another question: Did these people wear a uniform when they were coming to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you know whether they had normal belts or white belts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think they had white belts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after the war were you remunerated for this -- the confiscation of your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you never asked anybody to reimburse you for the value of your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. And I never heard of anybody doing anything like that or anybody receiving any reimbursement of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a follow-up question. Did you learn -- did you ever hear of any other cases where vehicles were seized? I'm not going to use the word "requisition," but did the military forces that were there, did they seize other people's vehicles to use for their own purposes, operations and so on, and then given them back, or was your an exceptional case where the vehicle was seized and never returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. There's no rule that says you can take somebody else's property and valuables and never give them back. That's something I've never heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened to your brother's vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: My brother had a heavy duty truck that he used for his work. He was a haulier. And it was devastated. It was probably used and destroyed. When it was running, they used it. When it was no use any more, they just left it in quite another area of the village, when it wasn't operational any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said "they" used it. Does that mean the military police, the "they," or the private individuals for their own purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no proof or evidence to say who used it, because there were a number of private citizens living there, Muslims -- or, rather, there weren't any more Muslims there and nobody could see who used them. They are best placed to know who used the vehicles and what they did with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, because you were speaking of Muslims who were there, I come back to the question I asked you a moment ago. When the vehicles were confiscated, were seized, or confiscated, to use your own word, were they only vehicles belonging to Muslims, or were they available vehicles belonging to various people? Because if I understand it correctly, those vehicles were used for certain activities and operations. So was it only the Muslim vehicles that were confiscated, or did they take any vehicles belonging to anybody else when they needed them, any other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whose vehicles were confiscated, whose were seized, except for my own. I know about my own case. And Ibro Kukic, I spoke to Ibro Kukic, who was in the camp with me, and I know he didn't give him the keys to his car or his own car, but they just seized it, used it. So in my opinion, they were property or other vehicles just taken away from Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that a third vehicle was confiscated belonging to Mr. Kukic, and you gave us a small -- told us a small -- a detail there that he didn't give him -- them the keys. Does that mean that those people who took the car didn't use keys but joined the wires to ignite the car, just like when a thief steals a car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how they managed to switch the motor on, to ignite the car, but I know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that Mr. Kukic told you that he didn't give them the keys. So if they didn't -- he didn't give them the keys, how were they able to set the vehicle in motion, to switch the engine on, motor on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they can forcibly take keys from someone, reserve keys or I don't know. I said, sir, that it wasn't Ibro but Himzo Kukic. Himzo Kukic was the name, whereas I heard the word Ibro. Ibro Kukic is Himzo Kukic's father.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it's Himzo Kukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well it was the vehicle of your brother, the Peugeot 305 which belonged to you, and the vehicle of Himzo Kukic, and we don't know which make it was. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the latter was Volkswagen. Because I was driven in that car from the schoolhouse to my own house when they wanted to search my home. The licence plate was Austrian because Himzo worked in Austria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, when the Judges ask questions they always dig up something new. So the Volkswagen had Austrian licence plates, and it belonged to Himzo Kukic. And that car was used to transport you when you left the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To take me from the school to my house on the day when they conducted the search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The day when they searched your house, who drove the Volkswagen Jetta with Austrian licence plates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Andrija Groznica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Poryvaev, when you're working with a paper, could you switch off the microphone, please, because it makes noises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say the driver of that Volkswagen Jetta that was confiscated was Andrija Groznica. Who was that gentleman? Was that a military police member, a civilian policeman? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had a military uniform on. I don't know what his duties were. It says here he was a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So is it the same man that we see in document 2131 that the Prosecution has just shown you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like to turn the witness to Exhibit 02177. This is a report of the mixed commission that visited Jablanica -- sorry, Capljina and Ljubuski detention facilities dated the 3rd of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, when you were in -- detained in Ljubuski, did you ever see any members of the joint commission that visited that camp?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you hear of such kind of visit of joint commission?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: I heard indeed that a commission was supposed to come, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to take a look at paragraph 11, which is in English version on page 4. In B/C/S version, on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: You mean item 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, item 11. Here according to the conclusion of the commission, individual prisoners complained about the attitude of HVO members when they were captured but not about --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, with your leave. I really don't understand this question. If the witness said he had not seen the commission, he had only heard that the commission was supposed to come but had never seen them, I don't understand the question, because this passage has to do with people who did see the commission. I do not see the purpose of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, what is the purpose indeed of your question? You want to establish what? Because the witness has just said he had never seen the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The witness was detained in Ljubuski for a certain period of time and the commission made some findings about the conditions of detention in Ljubuski and the manner in which detainees were treated there. So as a participant of those events, our witness may give some explanations whether the findings of the commission are consistent with the reality or not. That was the purpose of my exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if I may just intervene here. First of all, he can ask the gentleman what were the conditions, and he can get a narrative. That's the gentleman's actual testimony. Secondly, there are no conclusions from this report. It's a report. That's all it is, a reporting. But I think if the gentleman were to describe what he saw, what he felt, what he observed, that would be the evidence. Now, I don't think the Prosecution is going to have any difficulty in getting this report in. That's what I'm trying to say. These documents will come in because of the Rules of Evidence that we have adopted at this Tribunal. Then it's for them to dovetail. But to ask him about a paragraph of a report that was generated by some folks that he never saw, I don't see the evidentiary value in this. Now, I don't mind sitting here and going through all these documents, but then you can't have it both ways. Waste the valuable time by going through these documents when you can just get the narration from the witness. In 15 or 20 minutes the witness can tell us what he saw, what he observed, what he knows. That is his evidence. That's the best evidence. The documents can come in to support that evidence or to contradict it one way or the other. And it's up to us, the parties, to argue thereafter. I'm not trying to be difficult. I'm willing to just sit here like a potted plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: May I? Thank you. In order to help Mr. Karnavas, I would like only to ask a question from the witness about one paragraph, a particular paragraph of the report, and it is actually on page 4 of the report. In the English translation, in paragraph 10. And probably he may be able to respond to what I am going to read, of course with translation. And paragraph 10 says: "Among the civilians are 53 drivers from the area of Brcko, Tuzla, Zenica, and Novi Travnik who, in transporting goods for the needs of the HVO 108th Brcko and 115th Tuzla Brigade were stopped in Siroki Brijeg and thereupon detained in Ljubuski. Among them is a certain number of private entrepreneurs who have been detained, while their vehicles and freight have been confiscated." End of the quotation. Now, I would like to ask the witness if being there in the -- actually in the camp, did he meet any of those civilians who are mentioned here in the paragraph 10, what I just quoted, and those who had been asked to -- to transport goods for the need of the HVO, and also if he met those private entrepreneurs from whom their vehicles and freight have been confiscated. It is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did meet the drivers whose lorries and freight had been confiscated. What it says here is for the needs of the HVO. I didn't meet such drivers. I met Muslim drivers who had been supplying goods necessary for the survival of the civilian population. That was mainly foodstuffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I come back to the intervention by Mr. Karnavas, who normally gives us very valuable lectures on -- on the proceedings. This I did not quite understand, I must say. You have for the second time now in this series of questions to this witness suggested that the witness should tell the story, that he should be let to tell the story. This is a 92 ter case. The story is in the statement. We have it there. It doesn't have to be repeated in the courtroom. That, I would say, is a loss of time. On the other hand, I don't know how many times we have had the situation that one party either presented a witness -- a document to the witness in cases where the witness had no relation to the document whatsoever, but the contents of the document refer to something which the witness could say, "This corresponds to my personal experience," and I thought that what Mr. Poryvaev was doing was exactly in that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this opportunity. I don't want to waste too much time, but it's unfortunate and regrettable that you weren't here last week for a couple of days. I was fresher and probably more articulate at the time, but let me just exactly tell you what I said then. The statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I will read it. I will read it very carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The statement is coming in. I agree with you. That is his testimony, his direct examination. The Prosecution in advance can telegraph to all of us, including the Bench which paragraphs and which portions of document are relevant. The documents can come in. We would know, then, in advance what we need to focus on in our cross-examination. So this way you can circumvent a lot of this unless they need to go into something in particular where there is a need for narration. But that's my whole point. If we know exactly in which paragraphs they're going to ask the witness in a document that's 20 or 30 pages, that focuses everybody's attention that they're only interested in this paragraph. The document is coming in. But we seem to be moving in two different directions. 92 ter is turning into a regular direct examination. Barring a couple of exceptions, it's taking more time than what the rule was intended to prevent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my capacity as president of the Chamber, I subscribe to what Mr. Karnavas has just said. 92 ter procedure is geared at saving time. Otherwise, we would be hearing witnesses viva voce. However, if we are wasting time with documents that can be introduced through other witnesses or through other procedure, the 92 ter procedure is voided of its purpose. The procedure under 92 ter should be something that allows us to admit a written statement plus some documents that do not pose any problem whatsoever, but the substance of documents like this one, for instance, should be dealt with through another witness. Otherwise, we -- there is no point in -- in using 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that everybody understands this well, in the decision which is now pending concerning certification of appeal, we indicated unanimously, we the Judges indicated that it is appropriate for the Prosecution to bring in key witnesses who in that case would testify viva voce and could narrate what had happened to them and could also deal with documents of this kind. Our decision also made it clear that the Prosecution could complete some 92 ter witnesses and corroborate their evidence with 92 bis testimony. All this has been stated in our decision. And in the spirit of that decision, we need to have viva voce witnesses to whom we show documents of the importance like this one has, and through 92 ter witnesses we introduce some documents, additional documents, and through 92 bis witnesses we do not present witnesses. That would allow us, if we respect this procedure, to gain a significant amount of time, and that would justify the abbreviation of the time allowed that we ordered. That is all I want to say, Mr. Mundis, because all this fits very well together. Our decision was not whimsical, as you indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I thank the Presiding Judge for those comments. I don't have anything to add at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to finish, Mr. Poryvaev, therefore, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Poljarevic, I would like you to turn to still paragraph 11, item 11 of this document. And in this document, they say that the Croats were alleged to have been excessively rough when they captured inmates, whereas no one complains about how they were treated in prison. My question to you, Witness, actually were you excessively treated by the HVO soldiers when you were arrested in Jablanica -- sorry, in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were rough. They were rough. They beat me, and in my book that's called rough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Where did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: In the primary school building, in a small room when they were interrogating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who was interrogating you, and who was beating you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: The said gentlemen that we mentioned before, Ivan, and another man who was taking minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you mean Groznica?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: I mean -- I don't mean Groznica. I mean Ivan. They just called him Ivan. I don't know his last name. But judging by everything that I could see, he was leading that action, the attack on Sovici. I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any other Muslim men being beaten in Sovici while you were arrested in that village?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who was beaten?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Just, for example, I saw them knifing Muharem Helbet. They knifed him in the buttocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who did it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: They were uniformed soldiers. I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In what uniform were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Military camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Of which unit or troops?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, those were the forces probably of the Croatian army. The HVO, that is. It was already dark. I couldn't see everything, and I wasn't free to look around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are confusing us. You said it was either the Croatian army, the HVO, it was dark, "I couldn't really see." In your written statement, however, describing what happened on the 10th of April in the village, you said that you had seen HV insignia on the soldiers. Are you mixing these things up in general? How come that you could not distinguish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not confusing anything. I saw both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as insignia, I saw insignia of the Croatian army and of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite clear on that. You saw both types of insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were on the spot. We, the Judges, were not there. We are just trying to understand what happened. In your eyes, were there two different armies involved, the Croatian army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I saw, yes. I cannot give you the exact numbers as to how many troops were involved from which army. It was happening at night. There was no electricity in the village at all. It was a complete blackout, no lighting. I can't be sure that I saw everything very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your written statement you said that on the 17th of April, around 8.00, the HVO attacked the village of Sovici. A unit launched an attack from Jablanica. And you say at the end of that sentence that you saw HV insignia on the soldiers. So that was not at night. That was in the morning. The attack happened in the morning. During the day, in the afternoon, did you see HV insignia on the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, HVO units did not come from Jablanica on that day. They withdrew before they planned the attack. They mainly attacked from the village and from the direction of Risovac. They attacked from afar, first of all, and later in the evening when -- after the surrender, they felt more free and they gathered freely in the village because they had seen that everybody had surrendered. They had also information about the people who surrendered. And you could see more of them in the village that evening. And the next day on the 18th there were no longer so many of them because the majority had already surrendered and they had moved on, but still not far away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that there were not so many of them. You mean soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were not so many soldiers. There were less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately. Dozens, hundreds? How many units approximately? Can you give us a number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could say up to a hundred at that moment around the school building and throughout the village. You couldn't see a hundred of them in one spot, but they were in clusters, in smaller groups, up to a hundred of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, again continuing our conversation about paragraph 11. The commission made the conclusion that there were no complaints about the treatment of the detainees in Ljubuski. Is that correct? How were you treated in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: I personally was not beaten in Ljubuski, but there was very little room. The place where I was held was very small, and I was taken to do forced labour in the vicinity of Drinovac, in the area of Stolac facing Trebinje, and I was taken also to some private estates to work for some private individuals. The living conditions were very hard. There was a room not bigger than 4 by 2 into which 30, sometimes 40 people were crammed, and they were not allowed to get out at all except for maybe 15 minutes twice a day to get something to eat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Prosecution for once. This document that you are using, I see that it originates exclusively from the commission of the HVO, and there were three people in it, Davidovic and Kutlesa. There was supposed to be a joint commission including this Davidovic, Kutlesa and members of the ABiH, Pakuc, Hodzic and another one. How come that this document was not also signed by the ABiH side, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: First of all, the commission did not complete their job in Ljubuski because there were some circumstances when the Red Cross could not reach the area of Jablanica, and for this reason they quit the place. And we can suggest that members of the ABiH commission did not sign simply this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it's a document that comes from the HVO and is not a document of the two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The document was taken from Croatian archive, and that's why it's here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That wasn't my question, Mr. Poryvaev. What I want to know is that the document you're using with this witness is an HVO document, that's all. It's not an HVO-ABiH document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The document is called as a document of the mixed commission, but in fact -- in fact, the document is signed by the HVO part of the commission, only by them. It's a document which came from HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Well, for the transcript, that must be stated in more precise terms. The document was just signed by the HVO. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, you just told the Chamber that you were not beaten in Ljubuski, but did you eyewitness anyone being beaten in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who was beaten?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: I said Junuzovic, the one I saw being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: By whom was he beaten?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: He was beaten by those -- the guards, the guards of that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the guards?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the prison was Ante Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: To what military formation did he belong?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Ante Prlic? Well, I don't know which military formation. He was head of the camp in Ljubuski. So I don't know how else to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In which uniform was he dressed? What kind of uniform was he wearing, and what kind of uniform were the guards wearing?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms, patterned uniforms, and white belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at item 12 of this same document. In this paragraph 12, they say about people who were complaining of -- about injuries, and they say: "The commander of the Sovici battalion referred to an injury of his tooth and eye, while Muharem Cilic has an entry and exit wound of the upper leg. In addition, Ibro Kukic complained that he was wounded by a grenade while he was engaged in manual labour in Popovo Polje." When they say -- yes.

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did complain and asked for assistance which they were never given. I mean, medical assistance from a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When they refer to some commander of the Sovici Battalion, do you know whom they mean?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: I think they mean Dzemal Ovnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see him in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see his injuries?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know how he had got those injuries?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, while we were travelling from Sovici to Sovici, when the bus -- when the bus got lodged in the mud and we stopped for two or three hours, weren't able to move until a vehicle came to pull us out. We were stuck in the mud. So while we were waiting there stuck in the mud for the bus to be pulled out of the mud by this other vehicle, they beat Dzemal up. He was beaten up most. Other people were hit once or twice, but he was really beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know a person whose name is Muharem Cilic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see him in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see his injuries?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him that he got such kind of injuries?

utterances.speaker: ISMET POLJAREVIC
utterances.text: He tried to go from Sovici to Jablanica. He didn't want to surrender. There was several others in that group, and when they tried to escape the Croatians -- or, rather, the HVO soldiers shot at them, and that's how he was wounded. And today he has -- well, he's a very serious invalid today because the injuries were very serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, while I was listening to you, I was also reading the document, so I'd like you to tell me, because we Judges have to rule on the conditions of detention in that particular prison, so take a look at paragraph 4 of the report where it says that each prisoner had a bed, a covering, that you received three meals a day, that you were able to take a bath, and that you had access to various hygienic facilities and also received medical attention. So you who were there. What it says here, does that correspond to the reality of the situation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I can address the details now. Did you have a bed, you yourself, to sleep on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a covering of some sort to keep you warm? But as it was autumn and winter, perhaps it wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean while we were in Ljubuski or some other place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had, let's say, 10 blankets at the most for 30 of us in the room we were in. So we lived there. It was a 4 by 2 room, about 30 of us, and we had at most 10 blankets. We laid down on the ground. We couldn't even lie down. We were next to each other, so many people, one on top of each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you receive three meals a day? That is to say, breakfast, lunch, and dinner in the evening. Did you have three meals a day as it says here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the day we had two meals. Breakfast, which was just some sort of spread, and a cooked lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And as far as washing is concerned, was there any water, toilets, showers? Could you wash yourself or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Ljubuski there was just one toilet, and it was a terrible sight to behold. One for all the detainees. And we just washed once while we were in Ljubuski, and that was on the 17th of May. They took us by bus to Capljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when somebody was ill, could a doctor come and examine that person and prescribe any medication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this report it also says that they identified 42 civilians and 66 military men. The difficulty was that the military men didn't have any ID cards on them, but they did not come across anybody who was wounded and injured, with the exception of one particular person whose name was Omer Filandra [phoen], who had inflicted an injury on himself and was hospitalised.
